newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan firms warned not to set up China banks.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan firms warned not to set up China banks.

text.p: A senior Taiwan official on Wednesday warned local firms not to set up banks in rival China, a day after a visiting mainland official confirmed that one Taiwan company already had done so.

"Under the cross-straits relations act, Taiwan companies or individuals remain banned from investing to set up banks or financial institutions on the mainland," Investment Commission executive secretary Tsai Lien-sheng told Reuters.

"Any companies or individuals found doing so will be fined from T$3 million to T$15 million (US$110,000-US$550,000)," said Tsai, whose commission oversees all private Taiwan investment on the mainland under authority of the economics ministry.
Violators would be ordered to stop their China banking business operations or suffer continuous fines, officials said.
In serious cases, a company's Taiwan business license could be revoked.

Tsai issued the warning a day after a visiting China central bank official confirmed that one Taiwan firm already had invested US$80 million to set up a bank in Shanghai and that another had applied to do so.

Di Weiping, vice president of the Shanghai branch of the People's Bank of China, said China recently had approved a Taiwan firm's application to set up the first Taiwan-invested bank in Shanghai -- First Sino Bank.
Di, visiting with a group of senior economic officials, said First Sino was a Taiwan-China joint venture with Shanghai Pudong Development Bank with registered capital of US$100 million.
He welcomed other Taiwan firms to make banking investments on the mainland.
Di declined to identify the Taiwan investors.

Taiwan media have named First Sino's backer as Pou Chen Corp, a major investor in mainland footwear. They said Pou Chen owner Tsai Chi-chien and his brother Tsai Nan-feng had applied as private individuals to set up First Sino Bank.
The Tsais were unavailable for comment and Pou Chen executives refused to discuss the issue.
Tsai Lien-sheng of the investment commission said the government was checking whether Pou Chen or the Tsais had violated the law by setting up a bank in China.
"If it was true, they would be punished," he said.
Commission officials, however, acknowledged it would be difficult to punish First Sino's Taiwan financiers if they made their investments through offshore subsidiaries.
Taiwan has banned direct contact with China since a civil war split them in 1949.
In the late 1980s, it began allowing indirect trade and investment on the mainland, but banking and other major industries, including steel and power plants, remain barred.
Some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured more than US$30 billion on the mainland through third areas, principally Hong Kong, since the late 1980s.
